analysis.evidence: וּלְכָל חַיַּת הָאָרֶץ means ‘and to every beast of the earth’. The singular חַיַּת and the parallel phrases for birds and moving creatures show that the food is given to every member of the group.
analysis.morphology: Masculine singular construct noun with the prefixed conjunction וּ־ ‘and’ and preposition לְ־ ‘to’.

analysis.evidence: חַיַּת is in construct with הָאָרֶץ. The phrase וּלְכָל חַיַּת הָאָרֶץ means “and to every beast of the earth.” The verse lists these beasts alongside the birds of the sky and everything that creeps on the earth.
analysis.morphology: Feminine singular construct of the common noun חַיָּה, with no prefix or suffix.
analysis.sense: wild beast, beast of the field

analysis.evidence: חַיַּת הָאָרֶץ means “beast of the earth.” Its parallel, עוֹף הַשָּׁמַיִם (“birds of the sky”), identifies the earth as the realm these beasts inhabit.
analysis.morphology: Common noun, singular absolute, with prefixed definite article הָ־. It completes the construct phrase חַיַּת הָאָרֶץ.

analysis.evidence: In וּלְכָל עוֹף הַשָּׁמַיִם, כָל quantifies עוֹף ‘bird’. The phrase includes every bird of the sky among the recipients of food, alongside the land animals and the creatures that move on the ground.
analysis.morphology: Masculine singular construct noun with prefixed conjunction וּ ‘and’ and preposition לְ ‘to’.

analysis.evidence: In וּלְכָל עוֹף הַשָּׁמַיִם, “and to all the birds of the sky,” עוֹף forms a construct phrase with הַשָּׁמַיִם. It names a class of creatures receiving food alongside the land animals.
analysis.morphology: Masculine singular collective noun in the construct state, without prefix or suffix.

analysis.evidence: In עוֹף הַשָּׁמַיִם, “birds of the sky,” the sky is where birds fly, just as the earth is where the other creatures in the verse live or crawl.
analysis.morphology: Masculine plural noun in the absolute state with the prefixed definite article הַ־.

analysis.evidence: In וּלְכֹל רוֹמֵשׂ עַל הָאָרֶץ, כֹּל quantifies the singular participle רוֹמֵשׂ, ‘creeping thing’. The phrase extends the list of food recipients to every creature that creeps on the earth.
analysis.morphology: Masculine singular construct noun with prefixed conjunction וּ־ ‘and’ and preposition לְ־ ‘to’.

analysis.evidence: וּלְכֹל רוֹמֵשׂ עַל הָאָרֶץ means “and to everything that moves about on the earth.” The participle identifies the living creatures by their activity.
analysis.morphology: Qal active participle, masculine singular absolute, used substantivally.

analysis.evidence: In רוֹמֵשׂ עַל הָאָרֶץ, “moving on the ground,” עַל introduces הָאָרֶץ as the surface on which the creature moves.
analysis.morphology: Preposition without prefix or suffix.

analysis.evidence: In רוֹמֵשׂ עַל הָאָרֶץ, “creeping on the ground,” עַל introduces the surface on which the creatures move.
analysis.morphology: Definite article הָ־ + common noun, singular absolute, common gender.

analysis.evidence: אֲשֶׁר introduces the relative clause אֲשֶׁר בּוֹ נֶפֶשׁ חַיָּה, “in which there is living breath.” The suffix in בּוֹ refers back to the creature and supplies the “it” of “in it.”
analysis.morphology: Uninflected relative particle with no prefix or suffix.

analysis.evidence: In אֲשֶׁר בּוֹ נֶפֶשׁ חַיָּה, the feminine singular adjective חַיָּה ‘living’ modifies נֶפֶשׁ. The clause describes the animals receiving food as creatures in which there is life.
analysis.morphology: Common noun, singular absolute, with feminine agreement.

analysis.evidence: In נֶפֶשׁ חַיָּה, חַיָּה agrees with the feminine singular noun נֶפֶשׁ and describes it as living. The clause אֲשֶׁר בּוֹ נֶפֶשׁ חַיָּה identifies the animals in which there is life.
analysis.morphology: Attributive adjective, feminine singular absolute.

analysis.evidence: The phrases beginning with לְ identify the creatures receiving food. אֶת introduces כָּל יֶרֶק עֵשֶׂב, the food given to them. The governing verb נָתַתִּי (“I have given”) carries over from verse 29.
analysis.morphology: Uninflected direct-object particle with no prefix or suffix.

analysis.evidence: In אֶת כָּל יֶרֶק עֵשֶׂב לְאָכְלָה, כָּל quantifies the collective expression יֶרֶק עֵשֶׂב, giving the sense ‘all green vegetation’ as food for the animals.
analysis.morphology: Masculine singular noun in the construct state, with no prefix or suffix.

analysis.evidence: In כָּל־יֶרֶק עֵשֶׂב, יֶרֶק denotes the green growth of the herbage. לְאָכְלָה identifies that vegetation as food for the animals.
analysis.morphology: Masculine singular collective noun, unprefixed and unsuffixed. The absolute and construct forms coincide.

draft.change: Add the broader sense “herbaceous plant” to word 0 and use “herbage” as the article and word gloss. Retain the existing grass sense.
draft.definition: An herbaceous plant, or such plants collectively as herbage.
draft.evidence: Genesis 1:12 pairs seed-bearing herbage with fruit-bearing trees, echoing the command in Genesis 1:11.

analysis.evidence: כָּל יֶרֶק עֵשֶׂב means “all green herbage.” The phrase presents green plants collectively as food (לְאָכְלָה) for the land animals, birds, and creeping creatures listed in the verse. Nothing in the phrase singles out grass.
analysis.morphology: Masculine singular common noun in the absolute state, used collectively. It completes the construct phrase יֶרֶק עֵשֶׂב and has no prefix or suffix.

analysis.evidence: The animals are the recipients, and אֶת־כָּל־יֶרֶק עֵשֶׂב identifies what they receive. לְאָכְלָה states the purpose of the green vegetation given to them: it serves as their food.
analysis.morphology: Preposition לְ prefixed to a feminine singular absolute noun.
analysis.sense: food (what is given to be eaten)

analysis.evidence: In וַיְהִי כֵן (“and it was so”), כֵן refers back to God’s provision of green plants as food for the creatures. וַיְהִי reports that what God declared came to pass.
analysis.morphology: Qal wayyiqtol, third person masculine singular, with prefixed conjunction וַ־.

analysis.evidence: In וַיְהִי כֵן (“and it was so”), כֵן refers back to God's provision of green plants as food for the animals. The clause affirms that it came about as God had said.
analysis.morphology: Uninflected adverb with no prefix or suffix.
